messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Waiter/Waitress
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At forty-eight, Maria had spent most of her adult life moving through the world with a kind of easy confidence, the sort that comes from years of waiting tables in busy restaurants where you learn to read a room before you enter it. She had been divorced for nearly a decade, and while that had been painful, she had rebuilt a quiet life around her shifts at the diner, her small apartment with the garden window, and a handful of friends she saw for coffee or dinner. That life ended on a Tuesday evening in late October, when a customer who had been coming in three times a week for two months followed her to her car after her shift. He had left a note under her windshield wiper. The note was long and detailed, describing where she lived, what time she usually got home, and the color of the curtains in her bedroom window. He wrote that he had been watching her for weeks, that he knew her schedule, that he knew she was alone.

Maria called the police that night. They took a report, but the man had used a prepaid phone and a fake name on the diner’s loyalty card. He stopped coming to the restaurant, but the notes did not stop. They appeared on her car, slipped under her apartment door, once taped to the outside of her mailbox. She changed her locks. She started parking in a different lot three blocks away. She stopped walking home after dark. The police told her there was not much more they could do unless he made a direct threat. Maria began to feel as though she were living inside a nightmare that belonged to someone else. She would try to describe what had happened to her sister on the phone, but the words would not come out right. She could see the note in her mind—the handwriting, the way he had underlined the word *alone*—but when she tried to say it aloud, it sounded flat, like a story she had read rather than one she had lived. The memory felt alien, as though it had been dropped into her head from somewhere outside herself, and yet it forced its way into her awareness constantly, at the register, while she poured coffee, while she tried to fall asleep.

Over the following months, Maria became a person she did not recognize. She had always been someone who found joy in small things—the first sip of tea in the morning, a good tip from a regular, the way the light hit the garden window at dusk. That was gone. She felt dead inside, hollowed out, as though someone had scooped out whatever part of her had been capable of happiness. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. She went to work because she had to, but she stopped talking to her coworkers during breaks. She stopped returning calls from the friends she had socialized with before the event. Seeing them felt impossible; they would ask how she was doing, and she would have to lie, or worse, tell the truth and watch them not know what to say. She began to avoid any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. When a customer complained about a cold meal, Maria apologized and comped it without argument, even when she knew the food had left the kitchen hot. She could not bear the thought of someone raising their voice at her, of being noticed, of being watched with anger.

Her body had become a source of constant vigilance. She paid attention to her own physical state in a way she never had before—the tightness in her chest, the way her hands shook when she heard a car door slam outside. Strong physical reactions would surge through her without warning: her heart would pound, her skin would prickle with sweat, and she would feel a wave of nausea, all because a man at a nearby table had a similar build to the stalker, or because she heard footsteps behind her on the sidewalk. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home. Every creak of the floorboards, every rustle of the building’s old pipes, every car that idled too long on her street sent her heart racing. She avoided unfamiliar places entirely. She could not go to a grocery store she had never visited, could not take a different route home, could not agree to meet a friend at a new café. If she could not assess the danger of a place beforehand, she would not go there at all.

The consequences of these habits accumulated quietly. Her shifts at the diner became shorter; she stopped picking up weekend work because the parking lot was emptier and that made her feel exposed. Her income dropped, and she began to fall behind on her rent. Her sister stopped calling as often, tired of being met with silence or one-word answers. Maria knew she was disappearing, but she could not find a way back. She had come to believe that she was permanently broken, that the person she used to be was gone for good. What frightened her most was not the stalker anymore—he had stopped sending notes months ago, and the police had closed the case. What frightened her was the possibility that this was simply who she was now: a woman who could not feel anything, who could not trust anywhere, who could not remember her own life as something that had actually happened to her.

She came to the clinic on a Thursday afternoon, referred by her primary care doctor after a checkup during which she had cried without knowing why. She sat in the chair with her hands folded in her lap and said, very quietly, that she did not know if talking would help, but she could not keep living this way. She was hoping to feel something again, even if that something was pain. She was afraid that even that would not come.
